title: Impact of strain and dark states on spectroscopic measurements of silicon-vacancy centers in diamond
authors: Tommy Chin, Kesav V. Narayan, Imran Bashir, Kelsey M. Bates, Liam G. Stanton, Ehsan Khatami, Christopher L. Smallwood
abstract: Negatively charged silicon-vacancy (SiV$^-$) centers in diamond offer an attractive platform for the development of many forms of quantum technology. However, questions remain in connection to how large ensembles of SiV$^-$ centers behave in concert. Here, we develop a computational model designed to simulate recent experiments where optical multidimensional coherent spectroscopy (MDCS) was used to examine a high-concentration sample of SiV$^-$ centers in diamond, revealing significant variations in spectral signature depending on the detection scheme. Simulation results reveal that strain effects are highly random in this system, with a characteristic axial strain of $2.8 \times 10^{-4}$ and a shear strain of $3.5 \times 10^{-5}$. They suggest in addition that highly strained centers (with values exceeding $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$) may become significantly decoupled from optical emission. The results have implications for the use of SiV$^-$ centers as quantum sensors.
summary: This paper models the spectroscopic response of SiV- centers in diamond under strain using MDCS theory. By simulating measurements under different detection schemes (heterodyne vs. PL), the authors determined that random anisotropic strain best describes spectral broadening. The comparison between techniques successfully separates radiative from nonradiative decay pathways, providing critical insights for quantum sensing applications.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how strain variations and dark states affect the spectroscopic measurements of silicon-vacancy (SiV-) centers in diamond when using advanced techniques like optical multidimensional coherent spectroscopy (MDCS).
main_result: Fully random anisotropic strain best reproduces the measured spectral broadening, yielding characteristic axial and shear strain values. Furthermore, comparing heterodyne vs. photoluminescence detection separates radiative from nonradiative dynamics.
method: The authors developed a computational model using density-matrix perturbation theory within a Bloch-model framework, employing Monte Carlo sampling to average over random strain configurations.
model_or_system: The physical system is the negatively charged SiV- center in diamond. The model simulates MDCS signals by calculating spectral pole positions ($	ilde{\Omega}_{ab}$) that depend explicitly on six components of the local strain tensor ($\epsilon$).

main_assumptions: The analysis uses approximations like the impulsive limit and Markovian limit; a major limitation is that reproducing PL spectra requires an extremely high, potentially unphysical, ratio of nonradiative to radiative rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MDCS setup for both detection schemes (heterodyne vs. PL), the four-level energy structure of SiV-, and comparisons showing how fully random anisotropic strain best fits measured spectral lineshapes compared to structured strain models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework using density matrix theory, then applying Monte Carlo sampling to model ensemble averaging over strain distributions, and finally comparing the predictions from different detection schemes (heterodyne vs. PL) to constrain physical parameters like strain magnitude and decay pathways.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum system dynamics in solid-state emitters, using advanced spectroscopy to map out environmental coupling (strain) and identify non-radiative loss channels, which is central to building reliable quantum memories and sensors.
